Margins: who keeps how much of each dollar

Net margin = net profit ÷ revenue. A 10% margin means ₹10 of profit on every ₹100 of sales. ROA (return on assets) = profit ÷ total assets, and it splits exactly into net margin × asset turnover (revenue ÷ assets). A grocer earns 2% on each sale but turns its assets over many times a year; a chipmaker earns 30% but needs costly fabs. Two very different roads to the same ROA.

The middle bank keeps 16 cents of each revenue dollar; the middle builder keeps 4

Net margin per company, %: whisker = 10th–90th percentile, box = 25th–75th, line = median. Hover for loss-making share.

Source: Forbes Global 2000 (2026); company margins = profits ÷ revenue.

Two roads to profit: high margins (tech, pharma) or fast turnover (retail, food); banks have neither — they run on leverage

Aggregate net margin (%) vs asset turnover (revenue ÷ assets, log scale). Bubble = revenue. Dashed curves = constant ROA of 1%, 3%, 10%.

Source: Forbes Global 2000 (2026). ROA identity checked: margin × turnover = profit ÷ assets.

Valuation: what investors pay for a dollar of sales or profit

Price-to-sales (P/S) = market value ÷ revenue: how many years of today's sales the market is paying for. Price-to-earnings (P/E) = market value ÷ profit. "Aggregate" divides the sector's total market value by its total revenue/profit (big firms dominate); "median" is the middle company (tells you about the typical firm).

Chipmakers are priced at 8× sales; grocers and traders at under half a year's sales

Market value ÷ revenue, aggregate, by industry

Source: Forbes Global 2000 (2026); market value as of the list's April 2025 cut-off, financials FY2025.

Concentration: which industries are clubs of a few

Herfindahl–Hirschman Index (HHI) = sum of squared revenue shares (in %) of every firm in the group. 10,000 = one firm has everything; 100 equal firms = 100. US competition regulators treat above 1,800 as "highly concentrated" (2023 merger guidelines; older threshold 2,500). Here shares are within the Global 2000 only — not true market shares.

Beyond the 8 conglomerates, media and US drug distribution are the most top-heavy industries; banking is the most fragmented

Source: Forbes Global 2000 (2026); HHI and top-3 share computed on company revenue.

The real economy vs the corporate world

The World Bank splits the world's output and jobs into agriculture, industry and services. Map the Global 2000 onto the same three buckets and the farm sector all but vanishes.

Agriculture is 4% of world GDP and 26% of its workers — and essentially 0% of big-company revenue
